Because Vance is widely viewed as Trump's heir apparent for 2028, the disagreement has taken on added significance as a proxy fight over the party's direction and over who might lead it next. Trump's own position — publicly backing Vance's assessment while also redirecting Vance's attention away from Iran diplomacy toward domestic political messaging — adds ambiguity about the depth of any rift between the two.

stories.headline: Zelensky says US floated Donbas-for-NATO deal; Starlink restrictions also criticized
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Saturday that US peace envoys raised the possibility of Ukraine ceding the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, a proposal he said he would put to a referendum if it included robust security guarantees, no restrictions on Ukraine's military, and funds for reconstruction. The United States has not confirmed Zelensky's account; a US official told the BBC that “many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties.”

Zelensky’s remarks, released by his office, followed meetings this week between US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and both Zelensky in Dublin and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said. Hours later, Kushner urged “confidentiality,” described reported proposals as “maximalist,” and said private discussions were aimed at exploring ideas that might lead to “new proposals or breakthroughs.”

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that make up the Donbas. Moscow has insisted it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal includes Ukraine ceding control of those territories—including parts not yet captured—and the Crimean peninsula annexed in 2014. The Kremlin has also demanded limits on the size of Ukraine’s military, territorial concessions, and guaranteed neutrality, conditions Kyiv has rejected as leaving it vulnerable to future invasion.

Zelensky has long sought NATO membership, but the US and other allies have been wary, and Russia has cited NATO enlargement as a cause of the war. The Ukrainian leader said the idea was now “back on the agenda” as part of an “extremely difficult conversation” about European security. He warned that Moscow’s talk of a “new European security architecture” is a code for a weaker NATO and could lead to more conflict. “Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That’s it,” he said.

The comments add to recent tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Zelensky last week accused US officials of limiting Ukraine’s use of Starlink internet service, which it relies on for coordinating military operations. President Donald Trump responded by saying it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president” and called for fresh elections, which are suspended under martial law. Meanwhile, the European Union said it would include diplomats from Germany, France, the UK, and Poland in future peace talks, despite Moscow’s objection to European participation.

On the battlefield, Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces captured the settlement of Tersianka in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region and struck energy and transport infrastructure across Ukraine. Zelensky warned that Putin is “betting everything” on the winter campaign to damage civilian morale. The latest diplomatic exchanges were preceded by trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, where the Donbas-NATO proposal appeared to be a central topic.

stories.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting at APEC summit in China
body: The White House has announced that US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are planning a historic trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen next week. White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters the meeting would take place as Trump attends the two-day summit of 21 member states, and that the president intended to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons, whose proliferation he believes is very dangerous. It is understood Iran may also be discussed, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting; China has yet to react. No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday and will also hold bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday, their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025. Wales said Trump's trip, which includes an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific." The potential summit has already been dubbed a "new Yalta" by media, invoking the optics of the US, UK and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II to decide the new geopolitical power balance. However, analysts note that Beijing is uneasy about this framing and that China has deliberately remained vague in its public statements, with a Chinese Foreign Ministry official saying only that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties.

The meeting would come at a time when the world's biggest nuclear arsenals lack major guardrails, following the expiration of a US-Russia nuclear weapons control treaty in February. The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay, while Trump has said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that includes China, which has been building up its arsenal. Former senior US officials and analysts have said that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years. Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump, with the Wall Street Journal reporting that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.

China is in a delicate position as host. While Beijing and Moscow are broadly aligned on many issues, China does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm its efforts to present itself as a force for global stability. The European Union is wary of being left out of any Ukraine talks, and analysts say the trilateral meeting could trigger further escalation in already worsening relations between China and the EU if Ukraine is discussed without Europeans present. China has also been working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. Beijing has quietly provided Russia with a crucial market for energy exports and supplied technology and dual-use goods throughout the war, but officially maintains neutrality and has refused to take responsibility for the conflict's outcome.

Xi and Putin have met some 40 times since Xi came to power in 2012, and the two countries declared a "no limits" partnership in early 2022, weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The current Russia-China ties are deeper than they have been in decades, with a long-term strategy to contain US power and foster an alternative global order. However, analysts note limits to the alignment: Russian defense firms have accused Chinese companies of stealing intellectual property, Beijing is concerned about Russia's growing strategic relationship with North Korea, and the two countries differ on nuclear doctrine, with China maintaining a "no first use" policy while Moscow uses nuclear threats as part of its strategy. A US commission has described China as a "decisive enabler" of Russia's war, but also noted that intelligence and security concerns remain a constraint on deeper co-operation.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in bilateral talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting. Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit. For Russia, a three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Putin, who has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies since the invasion. For the US, standing alongside the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a difficult image, though Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term. For China, analysts say, even a meeting that yields only a photo opportunity could severely erode its image as a champion of the Global South and developing countries.

stories.headline: Iran claims drone attack on US base in Bahrain; Gulf states condemn strike
body: Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second such attempt in three days, the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said. The IRGC said it targeted a US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones. Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian attacks "before they could achieve their objectives". The interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location as sirens sounded across the kingdom.

The attack came after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September. The US military denied that the Friday strike caused any damage or injuries, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. Sunday's strike prompted a wave of condemnation from Gulf and regional states. Saudi Arabia said the attacks "constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness", while Qatar said the "continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension". Jordan and Egypt also strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows. Shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February. Iran insists it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states. Earlier this week, the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which US officials described as limited and defensive, in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response." Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at a press conference in Tehran on Sunday that Iran would continue to respond to any military aggression by the US or other states. Asked whether the strikes showed a change in Iranian direction as negotiations with the US have stalled, he said Iran was "not waiting for anyone" and was focused on its security.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports. This week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics. The IRGC also claimed on Sunday the sinking of an oil supertanker which hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, saying two ships had hit its mines while travelling through the strait, resulting in "massive explosions and fire". There was no independent verification of the claim.

stories.headline: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
body: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy linked to former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Singapore-based technology firm Megaspeed in August last year, the company said on Sunday. Megaspeed, the largest buyer of Nvidia chips in Southeast Asia, said it had launched an internal investigation following reports that questioned whether high-end AI chips may have reached China in violation of US export restrictions.

The scandal erupted after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia over alleged affairs with Alice Huang and an employee. Megaspeed is suspected of providing Chinese companies with backdoor access to Nvidia chips via its data centers in Malaysia, Indonesia, and Thailand. The United States has banned the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China. While Singapore does not enforce unilateral export controls imposed by other countries, it expects companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it was aware of reports containing "assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence." It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation." The company stated that it designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws, including US export control requirements.

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized the Commerce Department, led by fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips. Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process." The entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Howard Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export advanced chips. Other congressional committees have asked Lutnick and his department to retain all records related to Nvidia and Jensen Huang. China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

stories.headline: SpaceX catches Starship upper stage mid-air with 'chopsticks' arms
body: SpaceX successfully caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket on its return to Earth on Saturday, using mechanical arms nicknamed 'chopsticks' on the launch tower at Starbase, Texas. The spacecraft, the world's largest and most powerful rocket at 124 metres (407 feet) tall, had orbited Earth 14 times over 22.5 hours before descending through thick clouds, flipping to a vertical position, and slipping into the arms of the 'Mechazilla' launch tower. The catch marked the first time the upper stage of a mega rocket has been captured in midair, though the rocket's booster was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames after an earlier abort.

The manoeuvre required extreme precision: the spacecraft's engines were still roaring as the arms closed around it like massive tweezers, after which it hooked onto the tower and shut off its engines. 'That was the missing link, the holy grail of spaceflight,' said SpaceX mission commentator Dan Huot. 'We caught a Starship and now everything changes.' SpaceX founder Elon Musk posted on X, 'Ship 42 looks great!' and congratulated the team. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman called the feat 'almost magic' and said it was 'one step closer to [the moon].'

The catch came after a series of previous attempts. Since October 2024, SpaceX had successfully caught the rocket's boosters on three occasions, but the upper stage had never been captured. On this flight, the booster catch was aborted minutes after launch on Friday, and the booster was diverted to the ocean, where it burst into flames. The successful upper-stage catch is a milestone in SpaceX's push for full reusability, a goal that has driven the company's dominance in aerospace by slashing the cost of space travel.

The achievement has significant implications for space exploration. Niharika Patel, Technical Programme Manager at Loft Orbital, described watching the catch as 'magical' and noted that landing a rocket of Starship's size and weight requires incredible precision, autonomy, and the ability to withstand extreme re-entry heat. 'SpaceX has already significantly reduced the cost of getting to orbit through Falcon 9’s reusability,' she said. 'Starship takes this a step further by being a much bigger craft and aiming for full reusability of both the booster and the upper stage.' A fully reusable vehicle, she explained, can be rapidly refurbished and flown again, dramatically increasing frequency and reducing cost, essential for deploying large satellite constellations, building space infrastructure, and enabling sustained human exploration of the Moon and Mars. NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land astronauts on the Moon later this decade, welcomed the success.

stories.headline: Nvidia gears for pivotal earnings call after leadership crisis
body: Nvidia is preparing to report its third fiscal quarter earnings on Nov. 17, a day that has become one of the most anticipated on Wall Street after the stunning ouster of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang. The company’s stock has tumbled 24% since Oct. 29, when The New York Times reported Huang’s involvement with a woman believed by intelligence officials to be a Chinese spy, and subsequent reports revealed he had affairs with two company employees. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, leaving interim CEO Colette Kress, previously executive vice president and chief financial officer, to lead the earnings call.

Despite the turmoil, the underlying business remains formidable. Analysts expect Nvidia to report revenue of roughly $109 billion, an increase of nearly 50% from a year ago and about 13% from the second quarter. Earnings per share are forecast at $2.48, up from $1.30 a year ago. The company also recently announced a historic $150 billion stock buyback authorization. However, nine investment houses have downgraded their opinions on Nvidia’s stock, and two have cut their price targets. Shares closed at $162.85 on Nov. 13, down 12.7% for the year.

The leadership vacuum has raised urgent questions about Nvidia’s future. Rumors indicate that the board’s search for a permanent CEO has narrowed to three or fewer candidates, reportedly all external hires. Yahoo Finance Executive Editor Brian Sozzi suggested that the company should offer former Apple CEO Tim Cook whatever he wants to take the job for two to three years. Meanwhile, the board is conducting an investigation into whether Huang had additional affairs with direct reports and whether he divulged company secrets to the alleged spy. Investors are watching for clarity on both fronts, as well as the company’s long-term product roadmap and the viability of its annual GTC conference, which had been a showcase for Huang’s personal charisma.

The earnings call will be closely scrutinized not just for financial results but for signs of stability. Analysts are expected to press Kress on the China spying scandal, the company’s guidance under the new buyback plan, and any updates on the CEO search. “Nvidia is a very important company,” said Reddit co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman at Yahoo Finance Invest. “I am watching along with everybody else where this goes.” The broader implications extend beyond Nvidia: customers and neocloud providers such as CoreWeave have relied on Huang’s leadership, and a shift away from Nvidia chips could reshape the supply chain powering the AI infrastructure boom.

For now, investors are weighing whether to buy the bruised stock. Sozzi outlined several guideposts, including a definitive conclusion from the board’s investigation, aggressive share buybacks, a strengthened board with semiconductor expertise, and detailed product roadmap disclosures. “The Jensen premium is evaporating,” he wrote. “It’s hard to envision where the company will be 18 to 24 months from now.” The earnings call on Nov. 17 will be the first test of whether Nvidia can steady itself without the founder who led it for 33 years.

stories.headline: Bessent warns Fed against further tightening as rate hike debate intensifies
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday cautioned the Federal Reserve against further tightening of monetary policy, adding a prominent voice to a growing debate over the central bank's next move. The Fed is widely expected to raise interest rates at its Dec. 9 meeting, with CME FedWatch data showing an 86.8% probability of a quarter-point hike to a range of 4%–4.25% and a 13.2% probability of a half-point increase to 4.25%–4.50%.

Bessent's warning comes as markets have already begun reacting to shifting rate expectations. After October inflation came in hotter than anticipated, the two-year Treasury yield jumped about 18 basis points on Nov. 10, and the S&P 500 fell 0.38% that day. The index rebounded 1.3% on Nov. 11, helped by a rally in artificial-intelligence stocks. According to the fed funds futures market, there is a 100% chance the Fed will raise rates by at least another quarter point next month, following a quarter-point increase in September and a pause in October.

History suggests that the pace of rate increases matters more than the size of any single hike. A Charles Schwab study of more than a dozen rate-hiking cycles since World War II found that in "slow" cycles — defined as raising rates roughly every other meeting — the S&P 500 fell about 12% on average over the subsequent 12 months. In "fast" cycles — raising rates at nearly every meeting — the index fell by an average of more than 16%. The fed funds futures market currently expects the rate to reach 4.50%–4.75% by June 2027, which would put the current cycle in the "slow" category.

Past episodes show that the market's immediate reaction to a rate hike does not reliably predict its performance over the following year. On Dec. 16, 2015, the Fed raised rates by a quarter point for the first time in nearly a decade, and the S&P 500 gained 1.45% that day as investors had anticipated the move and the Fed indicated subsequent hikes would be gradual. On Dec. 19, 2018, a similar quarter-point hike coincided with a 1.54% decline, as investors worried about slowing growth and then-Chairman Jerome Powell signaled the central bank would continue reducing its bond holdings. Yet the S&P 500 gained nearly 28% over the next 12 months as the Fed reversed course and cut rates three times in 2019. In March 2022, the S&P 500 jumped 2.24% on the day of the first hike but lost 9.1% over the following year as inflation persisted and the Fed accelerated increases amid the Russia-Ukraine war and recession fears.

Bessent's intervention underscores the stakes for investors as the Fed weighs its next steps. Markets generally prefer slow, predictable changes; rapid increases create uncertainty that can turn investors defensive. One potential catalyst that could alter the Fed's plans is an end to the Iran war, which is driving energy-price inflation, though there is no indication a resolution is imminent. For now, the central bank appears set on a gradual path.

stories.headline: Australia thrash New Zealand to win fourth consecutive Rugby League World Cup
body: Australia defeated New Zealand 32-12 in the men's Rugby League World Cup final on Sunday, securing a fourth consecutive title and a 10th victory in the past 11 tournaments dating back to 1975. The Kangaroos ran in six tries to overpower the Kiwis in a one-sided final that never materialised into the gripping contest many had anticipated. The victory gave Australia a record-extending 13th Paul Barriere Trophy overall.

The result capped a tournament in which Australia faced persistent questions about the strength of their pack, following narrow wins against New Zealand (24-22) and Fiji (36-22) earlier in the competition. Superstar full-back Reece Walsh, who had been visibly unwell after the opening match following an eight-week layoff due to an ankle injury, delivered an impassioned response to the criticism. "I feel we got disrespected," Walsh said. "The chat from everybody coming into this tournament, everyone wrote us off, talking about how good all the other teams are and how good their coaches are."

Walsh, who acknowledged he was unfit for the first game after his rehab, praised head coach Kevin Walters for his belief. "It was hurting that first game. Coming off eight weeks of rehab, I was unfit, I didn't touch a ball but the belief Kev had in me, all the boys made my job so easy. To be out here now and win for Australia, I am so proud." Walters later paid tribute to veteran full-back James Tedesco, who captained Australia to victory four years ago and announced his international retirement immediately after the match. Tedesco, a three-time NRL Premiership winner and two-time World Cup champion, was brought on as a mark of respect and awarded the Clive Churchill medal.

New Zealand head coach Stacey Jones was blunt about his team's performance. "It was our worst performance. We got off to a bad start and could not fight our way out of it. When you make errors and your discipline is poor and give them all that ball, no matter what team you are it is just too hard." The Kiwis, appearing in their first final since 2013, were unable to deliver a twist in a tournament that also saw Australia's women's team win a record fourth World Cup title.

The 2026 World Cup, co-hosted by Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea, has drawn mixed reviews. The men's tournament was cut from 16 teams to 10, a decision that drew criticism from former England international Ryan Hall, who said the reduced format lost the "festival" feel of a World Cup. The group stage format, which featured one group of four and another of six with no quarter-finals, was widely criticised. England's men were the major losers: they won two of three group games but still failed to reach the semi-finals. Average attendance rose to 21,360 from 9,811 in 2022, helped by lower ticket prices (A$19, about £9.74) and strong support for Pacific nations. However, viewer access was uneven: Australia had free-to-air coverage, while UK fans could only watch the wheelchair final on BBC iPlayer and needed a Premier Sports subscription for other matches.

Japan, who struggled to contain England's pace and power, were ultimately outclassed. The 78-15 scoreline reflects England's superiority in all facets of the game, with the home side converting their opportunities with clinical efficiency.

The match was part of the Nations Championship. For England, the result provides a significant boost as they build towards future international fixtures, while Japan will look to regroup after a heavy defeat on the road.

stories.headline: FDA rejects Summit's ivonescimab lung cancer drug after trial misses survival endpoint
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has issued a complete response letter to Summit Therapeutics, declining to approve its experimental lung cancer drug ivonescimab for patients with previously treated, EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer, Summit announced on Sunday. The decision blocks the immediate U.S. launch of the PD-1xVEGF bispecific antibody, which had been approved in China since May 2024 for the same indication through Summit's partner Akeso.

In its letter, the FDA concluded that the drug could not be approved because it did not help patients live longer. While the Phase 3 HARMONi trial showed that ivonescimab plus chemotherapy reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 48% compared with chemotherapy alone, the agency stated that the progression-free survival benefit "in the absence of a statistically significant overall survival benefit does not support a positive benefit-risk profile in support of approval." The FDA specifically required a statistically significant reduction in death, and at the primary overall survival analysis, the hazard ratio in the Western subgroup was 0.98, indicating no survival benefit. Summit later submitted updated data showing an improved hazard ratio of 0.76 by June 2026, but the FDA apparently decided to stick with its overall survival requirement.

The rejection was not entirely unforeseen. Leerink Partners analysts had assigned Summit's bid a 40% probability of approval in a Nov. 5 note, citing the trial's failure to meet the overall survival endpoint. Before the FDA decision, Summit parted ways with its chief commercial officer Robert LaCaze and several senior commercial and marketing leaders who were tasked with building ivonescimab's launch plan. Despite the setback, Summit secured a $2 billion cash injection from AstraZeneca just weeks before the FDA's decision, providing the company with financial firepower to fund additional trials.

"We are disappointed for patients and their families awaiting additional treatment options in this setting," said Robert Duggan, chairman and co-CEO of Summit, in a statement. "We chose to pursue an ivonescimab regimen here based on the opportunity to provide another treatment option to help patients in need." Duggan added, "With five positive Phase III studies between Summit and Akeso, nothing changes with respect to our ever-growing belief in the opportunity for ivonescimab and our determination to advance ivonescimab's development."

The rejection narrows ivonescimab's potential first-mover advantage as several pharmaceutical companies—including Merck, Pfizer, BioNTech, Bristol Myers Squibb, and AbbVie—race to advance their own PD-(L)1xVEGF bispecifics into global Phase 3 trials. In the second-line EGFR-mutated NSCLC space, ivonescimab's absence reduces competition for TROP2-directed antibody-drug conjugates such as AstraZeneca and Daiichi Sankyo's Datroway and Merck's Kelun-Biotech-partnered sac-TMT, as well as Bristol Myers Squibb's dual-targeting EGFRxHER3 bispecific ADC. Attention now shifts to the all-important first-line NSCLC setting, where Summit's HARMONi-3 trial is ongoing; the squamous subgroup is moving toward a final progression-free survival analysis by the end of this year, and the nonsquamous group could report data in the first half of 2027.

Summit did not provide next steps for the EGFR indication in its Sunday release. The company formed around ivonescimab through a licensing deal with Chinese drugmaker Akeso, becoming one of the most prominent biotechs structured this way. Analysts have referred to the PD-1xVEGF class as a potential "Keytruda killer" after ivonescimab beat Merck's blockbuster in a head-to-head NSCLC trial in China, but Summit will need to secure dozens of indications to truly rival Keytruda, which is approved for more than 40 indications. Analysts expect the overall PD-1xVEGF market to reach $30 billion by 2032, while Evaluate has projected ivonescimab specifically at $4.4 billion for several indications by 2030.

stories.headline: US loses measles elimination status, health authorities say
body: The United States has lost its status as a country where measles is eliminated, a public health milestone achieved a quarter century ago, global health authorities have concluded. Researchers with direct knowledge of the deliberations told KFF Health News that the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) reached the determination this week, with a public announcement planned for Nov. 17. In public health terms, measles elimination requires that sporadic outbreaks end within a year, which is no longer occurring in the U.S.

Measles is entirely preventable: two doses of the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine prevent about 97% of infections, and when nearly everyone in a community is fully vaccinated, the virus cannot spread. Over the past two years, more than 830 people have been hospitalized with measles in the U.S., and more than 8,000 have been sickened in outbreaks that have cost an estimated $125 million in medical care, public health response, and productivity losses, according to Johns Hopkins University researchers. States have reported 13 measles-associated deaths, including a 7-month-old in New York and infants in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in recent months; babies typically are not vaccinated before age one.

PAHO, an international group that oversees health in the Americas and works with the World Health Organization, based its assessment on two analyses: one by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and another by an independent group of measles experts. Researchers had anticipated this conclusion after an outbreak in Utah surpassed the one-year mark in June. The U.S. had maintained elimination status since 2000, when the CDC and PAHO determined that measles was no longer a national threat, though occasional outbreaks sparked by travelers had been contained by herd immunity.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), Emily Hilliard, attributed the resurgence to vaccination gaps that opened years before the current administration, noting that childhood vaccination rates have steadily declined since the COVID-19 pandemic began. However, many scientists also blame the Trump administration for spreading vaccine misinformation and stifling a swift response to outbreaks. For example, the administration cut millions of dollars from state children's immunization programs and terminated funds for research on vaccine hesitancy. After Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. fired CDC Director Susan Monarez in August 2025, she told Congress she was fired because she would not preapprove changes to vaccine recommendations 'without reviewing the evidence.' stories.headline: Ebola outbreak reaches 11,145 cases, 5,437 deaths; Africa CDC says situation still out of control
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and neighboring countries has reached 11,145 cases and 5,437 deaths, according to the latest update from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on November 13, 2026. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) declared the outbreak six months ago and now says it remains out of control. The virus driving the outbreak is Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus, which has been reported in DRC, Kenya, and Nigeria.

Outside DRC, Kenya's Ministry of Health has confirmed nine cases and two deaths as of October 23. The initial case, reported October 6, involved a man who traveled from DRC through Uganda to Nairobi, where he was hospitalized and died in an isolation unit. Subsequent cases, including the second death, occurred among relatives and health care providers in close contact with him, all of whom were already in quarantine when diagnosed. Kenya has reported no community spread, and all cases were in Nairobi. Nigeria reported its first case in the outbreak on October 20, with testing confirming Bundibugyo virus. Uganda reported 21 confirmed and probable cases and three deaths overall; the last confirmed case in Uganda recovered and was released from care on July 16, 2026. France's single patient was released on July 4, and neither country has reported active cases.

The CDC reports that no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States and considers the risk to the American public low. However, travel restrictions remain in place: travelers who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight cannot board commercial flights to the U.S. Travelers from Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. Since 11:59 PM Eastern Standard Time on November 3, all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. must attest they have not been in DRC during the 21 days before departure. The CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces. Approximately 500 CDC staff are involved in the response, including more than 120 people deployed to affected countries.

The CDC cites limited health infrastructure, ongoing conflict, and frequent cross-border population movement as barriers to containment. Violence against health care workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to infections among health care workers treating patients. Mistrust of government and misinformation further complicate outreach. For U.S. clinicians, the CDC directs providers to its clinical guidance for Ebola disease, screening and diagnosis resources for viral hemorrhagic fevers, and infection prevention and control recommendations for U.S. hospitals. A travel history covering the prior 21 days remains central to identifying patients at risk.

stories.headline: SpaceX deploys Starlink satellites in Starship test, but booster crashes into Gulf
body: SpaceX conducted a test launch of its Starship rocket Friday night from Starbase, Texas. The vehicle deployed 26 satellites for the company's Starlink internet constellation, but its booster experienced a problem and was deliberately crashed into the Gulf of Mexico, according to NPR's Geoff Brumfiel.

The Starship upper stage is currently orbiting Earth and is expected to attempt a landing later today. The plan calls for it to re-enter the atmosphere, fly back to Starbase, and be caught midair by two mechanical arms on the launch tower. SpaceX aims to demonstrate rapid reusability for Starship, a capability the company says is necessary for its future revenue from launching thousands of Starlink satellites and eventually orbital data centers.

The booster's failed landing underscores the difficulty of the effort. Brumfiel noted that SpaceX is burning billions on Starship development and that shareholders will be watching what counts as success. The test is a critical step toward proving that Starship can be rapidly reused.

The test also has implications for NASA. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket, which currently serves as the only American vehicle capable of ferrying astronauts to the International Space Station. NASA has Falcon 9 launches contracted through 2028, but the station is expected to be crewed until 2030. Gwynne Shotwell, SpaceX's president, suggested at the All-In Summit in September that Boeing's Starliner capsule could fill the gap, but that vehicle has faced persistent technical issues and is not yet human-rated. Shotwell described Falcon 9 with a Dragon capsule as a "minivan" that is fine for short trips but unsuitable for a six-month journey to Mars.

stories.headline: Nvidia leadership crisis deepens after Jensen Huang's resignation; employees call for his return
body: Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 12th after a series of scandals involving extramarital affairs and a Chinese spying plot, triggering a leadership crisis at the AI chip giant. Nvidia’s stock, which closed at an all-time high of $239.24 on October 6th, fell to $162.85 on November 13th. CFO Colette Kress was named interim CEO, and Harvey Jones became the first board chair in the company’s history, signaling a possible restructuring of the unusual corporate structure where Huang had around 60 direct reports.

The crisis began on October 29th when The New York Times reported that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot involving Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. US officials believed Alice Huang may have been passing information to Beijing and that her company was illegally smuggling Nvidia’s AI chips into China. On November 6th, the Times reported that Alice Huang was specifically recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia’s CEO. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair on November 8th without naming her, prompting the board to launch an investigation. On November 11th, a second affair was reported with Nvidia VP of health care Kimberly Powell, one of his direct reports. By Thursday night, Reuters reported a third affair involving another Nvidia employee.

Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang raised national security concerns because Nvidia’s chips are considered critical to America’s AI superiority and are subject to export restrictions to China. Huang had reportedly misled Nvidia leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Alice Huang. Before resigning, Huang told people he felt “broken and shattered,” calling himself “a piece of shit,” according to Bloomberg.

Many in the tech industry and Nvidia’s own employees rallied behind Huang. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called it “a sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity.” Elon Musk said on X it would “be an honor” to hire him. Internally, Nvidia employees voiced support to “bring back THE boss.” Some speculated Huang was the victim of a coup or a conspiracy by China to chase him from the CEO chair.

The board’s investigation, which began November 8th, is ongoing. Nvidia faces a shareholder lawsuit claiming it deceived investors over the Huang relationship. Huang could face criminal charges if evidence emerges that he knowingly helped Megaspeed or other intermediaries illegally divert restricted chips to China, where a Culper Research report claimed over 20% of Nvidia’s 2026 compute revenue came from—a number not independently verified. The incoming Democratic majority in Congress is expected to tighten scrutiny on Silicon Valley and may impose stricter trade restrictions on Nvidia’s chips. The company has invested $99 billion in AI labs and plans to mobilize over $500 billion for data centers, making the scandal’s impact on the broader AI industry and US economy significant.

stories.headline: FAA ground stop caused by copper wire replacement, officials say
body: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday that a nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration on Friday was caused by routine maintenance work to replace outdated copper wire with a fiber optic line at a remote FAA facility. The upgrade, performed by longtime contractor L3Harris, led to a newly installed router flooding other routers in the Air Traffic Control system with more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, disrupting radar feeds and communication with planes. The ground stop was only the third such nationwide halt of the 21st century; aviation data firm Cirium reported more than 8,200 flights were canceled Friday evening, with at least another 3,000 canceled Saturday as effects continued after the stop was lifted.

Duffy told reporters the work was "routine maintenance" rather than part of a major modernization effort, noting the copper wire was so old it was being discontinued. He said the root cause remains unclear, citing possible faulty hardware, a misconfigured router, or "incompetence" on the part of L3Harris. FAA acting CTO Rebecca Guy said the agency saw two network locations pinging at a very high rate and disabled them to stabilize the network; a root cause analysis is now underway. Asked why the upgrade was performed at 3 p.m. on a Friday rather than late at night, Duffy said remote switchovers occur during the day, though he acknowledged there will be a reevaluation of when such work is done.

L3Harris said in a statement that it has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system in coordination with the FAA and its telco partners, with safety and reliability as top priorities. The company said it is supporting the FAA's investigation and takes the ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines, and air traffic operations seriously.

Duffy used the press conference to call on Congress for additional funding to modernize the Air Traffic Control system, saying lawmakers have given him only a "partial payment" to complete necessary work. The ground stop came a day after the FAA announced the rollout of an AI tool for air traffic controllers, but FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said there is "zero evidence of anything nefarious and zero evidence of anything AI-related," emphasizing the issue is a defective piece of equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, asked earlier whether AI caused the ground stop, replied, "We call it SI [super intelligence] around here, remember? SI."

stories.headline: SpaceX successfully catches Starship upper stage with 'chopstick' arms for first time
body: On Saturday, SpaceX successfully caught its Starship upper stage using the "chopstick" arms of its Mechazilla launch tower at Starbase, Texas, marking the first time the maneuver has been executed on the Starship vehicle itself. The catch occurred at around 4:20 PM ET after the spacecraft reentered from orbit, flipped vertically, and gently nestled between the tower's arms.

The Starship upper stage descended horizontally before three Raptor engines ignited to swing it vertical. Two small nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding about one foot, were the only purchase points for the tower's arms. The arms, known as "chopsticks," had previously been used to catch boosters, but this was the first successful capture of the Starship spacecraft.

The flight was not a complete success: the Super Heavy booster aborted its planned catch and detonated over the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX is investigating the cause. During the company's third-quarter earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said, "Success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight."

The achievement is a major step toward rapid reusability of the massive Starship system. Ars Technica noted that "this was a breathtaking feat" and that it felt "like stepping into the future." Unlike the Space Shuttle, which recovered solid rocket boosters from the ocean and did not recover the external tank, Starship is designed for full and rapid reuse—a goal that this catch brings closer to reality.
